sections.html: Alamogordo, the seat of Otero County, sits in south-central New Mexico where the Tularosa Basin meets the Sacramento Mountains. Holloman Air Force Base lies about 3 miles west of the city limits. Census figures put the town at 31,384 in 2020 and 31,906 for 2025, at an elevation of 4,330 feet. The base matters more to the housing market than anything else on that list, so most of this page circles back to it.

sections.h2: How Holloman Air Force Base shapes the housing market
sections.html:
Holloman is the largest employer of Alamogordo residents, and some estimates put the base at half of the local economy. The 49th Wing flies the F-16 and the Reaper and supports more than 21,000 military and civilian personnel. An older count from January 2008 showed 6,111 people employed directly on the base.

Two kinds of owners show up again and again.

  • Service families on assignment cycles. Orders land, a report date is fixed, and the house has to go whether or not the market is ready.
  • Retirees. About 6,700 military retirees live around town, and many have owned the same house for decades. When an estate or a move finally forces a sale, the house often needs work.

With a report date looming, a regular listing carries timing risk: showings, an appraisal, then a buyer's loan approval, and any of them can run late. A cash buyer has no lender to wait on, which lets the signing land on a date you choose.

Alamogordo is semi-arid, with 10.63 inches of rain in a typical year and roughly half of it coming in the July to September monsoon. Heat is the bigger wear factor. An average year brings 89.1 days above 90 degrees Fahrenheit, and about 55 winter mornings dip to 32 degrees or colder. Extremes run from 110 degrees down to minus 13.

Inspectors working in this climate usually start in three places.

  • The cooling unit. Evaporative and refrigerated systems both get a hard life here, and an old one is a probable repair request.
  • The roof. Dry heat bakes flat and low-slope surfaces.
  • Plumbing in an empty house. A freezing night can split exposed pipes if nobody is home to notice.

Snow is rare and seldom delays a closing, but repair requests do. When a cash buyer purchases the house as it stands, none of these items needs to be fixed first.

Otero County splits the yearly bill in two. Pay the first half by November 10 each year, with a grace period to December 10. The second half follows on April 10, with grace to May 10. You can pay by phone, online through the Treasurer's page, or in person.

The county Assessor decides what an Alamogordo house is worth for tax. The Treasurer then mails a single bill that rolls in the city, the school district and the state, so nothing arrives from city hall. Interest and penalty follow state statute, and the Treasurer's office can quote a payoff for your parcel.

A tax balance will not block a sale. Whatever is owed is subtracted from your proceeds at the closing table, alongside a mortgage payoff or a lien. Ask the closing agent for an updated balance shortly before you sign, because a deadline can pass mid-sale.

Start by pulling your most recent bill and confirming that both halves show paid. For an inherited house, also check whether earlier years are still open. Knowing the figure in advance keeps surprises away from the title company.

Alamogordo runs a Code Enforcement Division out of the police department, covering environmental and property ordinances. Anyone can report a dilapidated building by emailing the division, and empty or inherited houses draw the most reports.

If a notice is already on your door, deal with it or disclose it before agreeing to a price. For additions, garage conversions or new fences, call the Community Development Department, which handles engineering and planning and zoning. Buyers with a loan may ask to see permits. Cash buyers who accept the house as-is do not need that work legalized, though you should still tell them what was done.

sections.h2: Your options for selling a house in Alamogordo
sections.html:
There are three ways to go, and they differ in cost, effort and speed.

  • Hire an agent: the widest exposure, paid for with a commission and a wait through repairs, appraisal and the buyer's loan.
  • Sell by owner: you keep the commission and take on the showings, disclosures and paperwork.
  • Sell for cash: no lender and no appraisal condition, with a closing date the buyer can fit to your schedule.

Expect a cash offer to land under what a fully repaired house might bring on the open market, and we will not name a number before seeing the property. You are paying for speed and certainty. Cash tends to suit inherited houses, tenant-occupied rentals, homes that need roof or cooling work, and owners with a firm moving deadline.

Around Holloman, a good share of houses have one owner for a long stretch, then pass to heirs who live elsewhere. Those heirs usually want a clean exit without driving to Otero County for every showing or repair visit. A cash purchase fits that case because one buyer inspects once, agrees on a price, and handles the rest through the title company.

Bring whatever proves you can sign: probate papers, or the deed if the house is already in your name. Tell the buyer about leaks, an older cooler or any city notice. Plain disclosure up front shortens the negotiation and keeps the closing date from moving.

sections.h2: A simple order of steps for a quick sale
sections.html:
Most owners with a deadline follow the same sequence. First, find your move date or report date and work backward. Second, gather the deed, a mortgage statement and the latest Otero County tax bill. Third, walk the house with a cooling, roof and plumbing checklist so nothing surprises you later. Fourth, compare a listing timeline with a cash timeline and decide which one fits the date. Last, choose a title company, confirm in writing who covers each cost, and schedule the signing.

If the house is a rental, mention the tenant situation early. An occupied house changes showings and the closing date, and a buyer who knows up front can plan around it.

Closing runs through a title company whichever route you take. Staff there confirm ownership, collect any unpaid tax, pay your mortgage and liens from the proceeds, and record the deed. You sign, hand over the keys, and receive the balance.

Bring the deed or probate papers, your latest tax bill, a mortgage statement if you have a loan, and permit records for any work on the house. Get the offer in writing, and settle who pays each closing cost before you agree to anything.

faqs.a: Alamogordo is the seat of Otero County in south-central New Mexico, in the Tularosa Basin below the Sacramento Mountains, with Holloman Air Force Base just to the west.

faqs.q: When are Otero County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Half is due November 10, with payment still timely through December 10. The other half is due April 10, timely through May 10.

faqs.q: Does Holloman Air Force Base affect selling a house in Alamogordo?
faqs.a: Yes. Being the top employer of local residents, the base produces a steady stream of assignments and retirements, which creates sellers and buyers alike.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Alamogordo with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes. Cash buyers can accept the house as-is, and any open notice is cleared at or before closing. Mention it at the first conversation.

faqs.q: Who values and bills property tax in Alamogordo?
faqs.a: The Otero County Assessor sets the value and the Otero County Treasurer bills and collects. Alamogordo sends no separate property tax bill.
